clue.text: He's always on strike at Westminster

definitions.text: He's always on strike at Westminster

parts.words: He's always on strike at Westminster
parts.note: read as a trade unionist forever walking out in Parliament, but it means the great bell whose hammer strikes the hours over the Palace of Westminster

explanation.walkthrough: 'On strike' suggests industrial action; here it is a clock bell being struck every hour. The famous bell in the Houses of Parliament clock tower.
explanation.definitionFit: The great hour bell in the Elizabeth Tower at Westminster is struck by its hammer continually, chiming every hour.

clue.text: Its music can, put, jumpy people in a transport

definitions.text: Its music can, put, jumpy people in a transport

parts.words: Its music can, put, jumpy people in a transport
parts.note: a transport is both a vehicle and a state of rapture; people eager to join a popular cause jump on the vehicle carrying the musicians

explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' means both rapture and a vehicle; to jump on this vehicle is to join a fashionable cause.
explanation.definitionFit: A cart carrying a band in a parade gave us the idiom of joining a popular movement for advantage.

clue.text: Grant for one didn't fancy caviare

definitions.meaning: Ulysses S. Grant commanded the Union army in the American Civil War
Hamlet's line 'caviare to the ...' means too refined for the common public

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like a gift; it is the American commander. Shakespeare's 'caviare to the general' means the populace never relished delicacies.
explanation.definitionFit: Grant was a Civil War commander of top rank, and Hamlet uses the word for the populace that dislikes caviare.

clue.text: Rackstraw's one recommendation

parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore the sailor Ralph Rackstraw is praised in a song for his nationality, 'it is greatly to his credit'

explanation.walkthrough: In HMS Pinafore the chorus sings that Ralph Rackstraw is a native of England, and 'it is greatly to his credit': his one recommendation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pinafore song says his English birth is greatly to his credit, so his nationality is what commends him.

clue.text: One of the big cats that has its toll

definitions.text: One of the big cats that has its toll

parts.words: One of the big cats that has its toll
parts.note: a big tomcat would be a large male cat, but here the 'tom' is the great bell of Christ Church, Oxford, which tolls each night

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big cats' points to lions and tigers; the joke is a huge tomcat. The Oxford bell in Tom Tower, Christ Church, tolls 101 times each evening.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Christ Church bell in Oxford shares a name with a large male cat, and a bell tolls.

clue.text: Standing-in for salesman doing up his shoes '

parts.note: rep, short for representative, is a travelling salesman
lacing is tying shoelaces

explanation.surface: A substitute salesman stops to tie his shoelaces.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking another's place is substituting for them, standing in for that person.

clue.text: A cry of distress, from Central Asia

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A wail of anguish comes from the heart of Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an exclamation of grief or regret, a cry of sorrow.

clue.text: Day for emptying barrels. Night for play

definitions.meaning: the Glorious ..., 12 August, opens the British grouse-shooting season when gun barrels are fired
Shakespeare's comedy is titled with this word followed by Night

explanation.walkthrough: 'Emptying barrels' suggests drinking; it is firing guns on 12 August, the start of grouse shooting in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Glorious Twelfth of August opens grouse shooting, and Shakespeare's comedy is named after the Epiphany eve.

clue.text: He is very much attached to his Penny

definitions.text: He is very much attached to his Penny

parts.words: He is very much attached to his Penny
parts.note: Penny looks like a sweetheart's name, but it is the coin: a hoarder cannot bear to part with money

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Penny' a girlfriend; it is the coin a skinflint clings to.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder of money cannot bear to spend even the smallest coin, clinging to every one.

clue.text: Hitch horse to bottom of pole

parts.note: the South pole is at the bottom of a globe, so S
a nag is a horse

explanation.surface: Someone ties a horse to the base of a post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hitch' looks like tethering; it means a problem. The south pole is at the bottom of the globe, giving S.
explanation.definitionFit: A snag is an unexpected difficulty, as is a hitch.

clue.text: Not the Greek games of a number of Angles

parts.note: non is the Latin and French negative, used in English as a prefix meaning not
agon was the ancient Greek word for a contest or public games

explanation.surface: Someone declines the Greek games in favour of a group of Angles, the old English tribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angles' is capitalised to suggest the Germanic tribe; it means geometric angles, nine of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A nine-sided plane figure has nine corners, so it has a set number of angles.

clue.text: Poddy Partlets ?

parts.note: Partlet is the traditional name for a hen (Chaucer's Pertelote), and 'Poddy' suggests something that grows in a pod, like a garden pea

explanation.walkthrough: Partlet is the hen in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale, so it stands for any hen; 'poddy' hints at the pea pod, giving a fanciful pea-hen.
explanation.definitionFit: Female peafowl are literally hens of the pea, and the clue jokes that pod-grown hens would be so called.

clue.text: With which Mrs Bardell made things hot for the retiring Pickwick?

definitions.text: With which Mrs Bardell made things hot for the retiring Pickwick?

parts.words: With which Mrs Bardell made things hot for the retiring Pickwick?
parts.note: Mrs Bardell, Mr Pickwick's landlady in Dickens, 'made things hot' for him by suing him, but a landlady would also heat the bed of a lodger retiring for the night

explanation.walkthrough: In The Pickwick Papers Mrs Bardell sues Pickwick for breach of promise. 'Retiring' means going to bed, and the long-handled pan of hot coals warmed the sheets.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered pan of embers on a long handle was run between the sheets to heat a bed before someone slept in it.

clue.text: Says he's pro Cymru

parts.note: a Welshman who declares '...', that is 'I am pro', is giving his own Welsh first name; Cymru is the Welsh name for Wales

explanation.walkthrough: The Welsh form of Ivor sounds like a man saying 'I for', meaning 'I am in favour'. Cymru is Welsh for Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common Welsh man's name, the Welsh equivalent of Ivor, so it suits someone from Wales.

clue.text: Their branches are lightly burdened

parts.note: branches suggest trees, but these are the arms of a branched holder carrying candles, so they bear light

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lightly burdened' seems to mean carrying little weight; it means bearing lights.
explanation.definitionFit: Large branched candlesticks hold several candles on their arms, so each arm carries a light.

clue.text: Honourable companion in the red : they're deep

indicators.note: the companion is placed inside the red, so the abbreviation sits within the heraldic word

parts.note: gules is the heraldic term for red
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A distinguished companion of the realm finds himself in the red, deep in debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the red' suggests overdraft; here red is the heraldic colour GULES, with CH put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Gulches are steep narrow ravines, so they are deep clefts in the land.

clue.text: Namely she who arrived when Wenceslas' went out ?

definitions.text: Namely she who arrived when Wenceslas' went out ?

parts.words: Namely she who arrived when Wenceslas' went out ?
parts.note: Good King Wenceslas looked out on the Feast of Stephen; a girl born that day would bear the saint's name in feminine form, and namely is i.e.

explanation.walkthrough: The carol: Wenceslas 'looked out on the feast of Stephen', 26 December. 'Namely' is IE, the ending tacked on the saint's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This feminine form of Stephen would suit a girl born on St Stephen's Day, when the carol king looked out.

clue.text: Terrible weedkiller of Waverley

parts.note: Ivan the Terrible was the Russian tsar, so the epithet points to his first name
a hoe is the garden tool used to kill weeds

explanation.surface: A dreadful herbicide is found in Waverley, perhaps the Edinburgh station.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's novels are called the Waverley novels, after the first of them; this one is his tale of medieval England.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's novels are known collectively as the Waverley novels, and this chivalric romance is one of that series.

clue.text: Wood product. 'Stanley ruined one, nothing less

indicators.note: ruined tells us the letters of the name and what remains are wrecked and rearranged
less means the following thing is taken away from the word one

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A carpenter called Stanley spoiled one piece of woodwork, nothing less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' is Mrs Henry Wood, Victorian author. ONE less O (nothing) gives NE; 'ruined' scrambles STANLEY with NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Henry Wood wrote this sensational 1861 Victorian novel, so it is a product of Wood's pen.

clue.text: Hastened back with speed to tell the tale

indicators.note: back tells us the word for hastened is written from right to left

parts.note: ran means hastened
rate means speed, as in a rate of knots

explanation.surface: Someone hurried home quickly to recount the story.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to give an account of events in order, the same as recounting a story.

clue.text: Bony cage takes a weight of apple

parts.note: the ribs form the bony cage of the chest
a ton is a weight

explanation.surface: A ribcage is weighed down by apples.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ribston Pippin is an old English apple variety from Ribston Hall, Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ribston Pippin is a traditional English dessert variety of this fruit.

clue.text: She's worshipped by Desmond. in the gallery

indicators.note: Desmond is placed in the gallery, so the short name goes inside the word for the cheap seats

parts.note: the gods is the top gallery of a theatre
Des is the short form of the name Desmond

explanation.surface: Desmond, up in the theatre gallery, adores a woman on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The gods' is the highest, cheapest gallery in a theatre; DES goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A female deity is the object of worship, so she is the one worshipped.

clue.text: Foreign entitlement F.N.D. say, spell that out

indicators.note: say and spell out ask for the letters to be pronounced by their names, as they are heard

parts.note: the letter names F, N, D spoken are EF, EN, DEE

explanation.surface: A foreign title abbreviated as F.N.D. needs spelling out in full.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, the letter names F, N, D run together into the Turkish title of respect.
explanation.definitionFit: It was a Turkish title of respect for officials and scholars, an honorific from abroad.

clue.text: I reach Slough returning by desert route

indicators.note: returning turns the whole run of I and the swamp word round, so it reads back to front

parts.note: a slough is a bog or marsh

explanation.surface: A traveller reaches the town of Slough on the way back from a desert journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slough' looks like the English town; it is a swamp, BOG. 'Returning' reverses I plus BOG to give the Mongolian desert.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Asian expanse of the Gobi in Mongolia and China is one of the world's largest deserts.

clue.text: If you have the gift of it, continue, in Africa

parts.words: If you have the gift of it
parts.note: having the gift of the gab is being able to talk fluently, so gab
on means continue, as in carry on

explanation.surface: Someone with a talent is urged to keep going across Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'gift of the gab' is talking easily. 'In Africa' defines the West African country.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabon is a West African country on the Atlantic coast, so it is located in Africa.

clue.text: Kiss tot of Pan's ?

parts.note: in Peter Pan, Wendy offers a kiss and Peter, not knowing the word, is given a thimble instead, which Wendy then calls a kiss; a tot is a small measure of drink

explanation.walkthrough: In Barrie's Peter Pan a thimble stands for a kiss, so a small tot, a tiny measure, is a 'kiss's worth' in Pan's language.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny measure of drink is as much as a sewing thimble holds, and in Peter Pan a thimble stands for a kiss.

clue.text: Underground worker goes to sea

definitions.meaning: a burrowing animal or a spy working undercover
a stone breakwater or pier extends out into the sea

explanation.walkthrough: A 'mole' is the burrowing animal and also a stone pier or breakwater reaching out into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A burrowing mammal works underground, and a harbour breakwater stretches out from the shore into the sea.

clue.text: Used sense in choice of material

definitions.meaning: the past tense of feel, using the sense of touch
a matted woollen fabric used as cloth

explanation.walkthrough: One meaning is the past tense of feel; the other is the pressed woollen cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Touch is a sense, so having used it you touched something; the cloth is a pressed wool fabric.

clue.text: Intermediately wager a little'n

parts.note: bet means wager
a little one, little (WEE) plus 'n, a clipped one or N

explanation.surface: Someone places a modest bet on a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little'n' is a dialect 'little one': WEE (little) with 'N, the clipped 'one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something placed in an intermediate position lies in the middle of two others.

clue.text: Source of Solomon's building material

parts.note: King Solomon built his temple with cedar wood sent from King Hiram's forests to the north

explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible (1 Kings 5) Solomon builds the Temple with cedars from the forests of this land.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible records that Hiram of Tyre sent cedar timber from that country for Solomon's temple in Jerusalem.

clue.text: The last hundred, to date

parts.note: the hundred most recent years, up to the present date, are the years beginning with this figure followed by hundred

explanation.walkthrough: Written in the twentieth century: the current hundred years, 'to date', are all dated with this number before 'hundred'.
explanation.definitionFit: Every year of the twentieth century begins with this figure, so it is the number heading the present hundred years.

clue.text: Art rumour? One like 15

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist, so it stands for art
the grapevine is the route of rumour, so vine can mean rumour

explanation.surface: Gossip in the art world is like a deep cleft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One like 15' points back to 15 Across, GULCHES: a deep narrow valley.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep narrow gorge is the same sort of landform as a gulch.
